What follows is a preliminary analysis of mono- and disyllabic lexical items; no attempt has yet been made to investigate tone in discourse. Tone is not generally marked in the new orthography, since no contrasts exist in ‘minimal trios’ and those in ‘minimal pairs’ can be distinguished in context. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Tera is described as a lexical tone language with three level tones (H, M, L) on every syllable; neither Tench 2007 nor Newman 1964 says anything about word stress or accent, so no stress placement rule is on record in the accessible primary descriptions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone notes only: no HL/LH on disyllables; mid tone partially assimilates to neighbouring H or L; possible voicing-tone interaction (voiced obstruents favour L).
new_statements.domain_note: Both descriptions treat isolated lexical items (mono- and disyllables); Tench explicitly has not analysed tone in discourse, Newman fn.7 likewise for longer utterances. Silence on stress is silence, not a claim that stress is absent.
new_statements.identity_note: Tench 2007 describes the 'standard' Tera of radio news, from speakers of Deba, Hinna, Difa, Zambuk and Lubo (Gombe State); Newman 1964/1970 are based on one speaker from Wuyo (eastern Tera area). Same language, tera1251; Newman notes Tera and Pidlimdi (Hinna) form one dialect cluster.
